day1.instructionsForPlatform: Conceptual multiple choice. Delivered through Pear Assessment (formerly Edulastic) — this is an item bank to copy into the platform, not a printed page. A demo set of 8 items is built here to prove the parallel-version mechanic; the real test runs ~25 items per DECISIONS.md and scales the same way.

items.learningTarget: Define the mole as a counting unit (S7.2)
items.stem: A mole is best described as which of the following?
choices: A unit of mass equal to one gram
The atomic number of an element
A fixed number of particles, the way a dozen is a fixed number of eggs
A unit that only applies to gases
distractorRationale: Confuses the mole (a count) with grams (a mass) — the exact mix-up the unit's key idea warns against.
Confuses mole with atomic number; no relationship between the two.
Overgeneralizes from the gas-at-STP conversion to all moles.

items.stem: One mole of any substance contains how many particles?
distractorRationale: 22.4 L/mol is the molar volume of a gas at STP, not a particle count — a real mix-up between two constants introduced the same week.
1.008 is the atomic mass of hydrogen in g/mol, not Avogadro's number.
Right form, wrong exponent — catches a student who half-remembers the number.

items.stem: To find the molar mass of a compound, you should:
choices: Add the atomic numbers of every element in the formula
Multiply the molar masses of the elements together
Use only the molar mass of the first element listed
Add the molar mass of every atom in the formula, multiplying by each subscript
distractorRationale: Confuses atomic number (periodic table position) with atomic mass (the g/mol value actually needed).
Molar masses are summed, never multiplied — a made-up operation with no chemical meaning.
Ignores every atom but one; would give a real student a wildly low answer on Ca(NO₃)₂-type formulas.

items.stem: In Ca(NO₃)₂, how many total oxygen atoms are present?
distractorRationale: Reads only the inner subscript on O and forgets the outer 2 multiplies it.
Confuses the outer subscript (which multiplies the whole NO₃ group) with the oxygen count directly.
Adds the two subscripts (3 + 2 × 3) instead of multiplying them.

items.stem: A student wants to convert 10.0 g of a compound directly into a number of molecules in one step. What is wrong with that plan?
choices: Grams and particles never convert directly — the calculation has to pass through moles first
Nothing is wrong; grams convert directly to particles using Avogadro's number
Grams can only be converted to liters, never to particles
The conversion is only possible for gases at STP
distractorRationale: This is the exact misconception the unit's key idea targets — skipping the mole step entirely.
Confuses this conversion pathway with the STP gas-volume pathway, which is a separate route.
Wrongly restricts a general rule (all grams-to-particles conversions) to one special case (STP gases).

items.stem: Which conversion factor correctly turns a known mass in grams into moles?
choices: mass (g) × molar mass (g/mol)
mass (g) ÷ 22.4 L/mol
mass (g) ÷ molar mass (g/mol)
distractorRationale: Inverts the operation — multiplying instead of dividing gives units of g²/mol, which do not cancel to moles.
Divides by Avogadro's number instead of molar mass — confuses two different conversion factors.
Uses the STP molar-volume constant on a mass, not a volume — units do not cancel to moles.

items.stem: After setting up a mole-conversion problem, the units do not cancel to the unit the question asked for. What does that mean?
choices: It does not matter, as long as the final number looks reasonable
The setup is wrong and needs to be redone — not just the arithmetic
Round the answer so the units match anyway
Units only need to cancel on gas problems
distractorRationale: This is the exact shortcut the unit tells students not to take — the key idea is stated as a warning against it.
Rounding cannot fix a units problem; the setup itself is the error.
The rule applies to every mole conversion, not only STP gas problems.

items.learningTarget: Sample size vs. amount of substance (S7.2)
items.stem: Sample X is 1.00 mol of helium gas. Sample Y is 1.00 mol of lead. Which contains more atoms?
choices: Sample X, because gases have more particles per mole
Sample Y, because lead is denser
Neither — both contain the same number of atoms
It cannot be determined without knowing the volume
distractorRationale: Confuses particle count (fixed by the mole) with physical state — gases do not get "extra" particles per mole.
Confuses density (a mass-per-volume property) with particle count, which the mole fixes regardless of density.
Volume is irrelevant to particle count once the amount in moles is already known.

items.learningTarget: Define the mole as a counting unit (S7.2)
items.stem: Which statement best defines a mole?
choices: A measurement of an object's mass in grams
The number of protons in an atom's nucleus
A counting number equal to 6.022 × 10²³ of something, the way "dozen" means 12
A unit used only when measuring liquids
distractorRationale: Confuses the mole (a count) with grams (a mass).
Confuses mole with atomic number/proton count.
Wrongly restricts the mole to one state of matter.

items.stem: Avogadro's number is used to convert between moles and:
choices: Number of particles
Volume in liters
Mass in grams
Atomic mass units
distractorRationale: Volume converts through 22.4 L/mol at STP, a different constant entirely.
Mass converts through molar mass, a different constant entirely.
Atomic mass units describe one atom, not a mole-scale sample.

items.stem: The molar mass of a compound is found by:
choices: Averaging the atomic masses of the elements present
Adding the atomic numbers of every element in the formula
Using the molar mass of only the heaviest element
Summing each element's molar mass, multiplied by its subscript in the formula
distractorRationale: Averaging instead of summing loses the effect of the subscripts entirely.
Confuses atomic number with atomic mass.
Ignores every atom but one, badly underestimating polyatomic compounds.

items.stem: In Mg(OH)₂, how many total hydrogen atoms are present?
distractorRationale: Reads the inner formula but forgets the outer subscript multiplies it.
Doubles the wrong part of the formula — multiplies the O count instead of the whole group correctly.
No basis in the formula; a guess between the two nearby numbers.

items.stem: Why can't grams be converted straight to number of particles in a single step?
choices: Because there is no direct conversion factor between grams and particles — moles are the required middle step
Because grams only apply to solids
Because particles can only be counted for gases
Because the calculation would require calculus
distractorRationale: Grams describe mass for any state of matter, not only solids.
Particle counts apply to any sample, not only gases.
The math involved is arithmetic, not calculus — an irrelevant reason.

items.stem: To convert a known number of moles into a mass in grams, you should:
choices: Divide moles by molar mass (g/mol)
Multiply moles by 6.022 × 10²³
Divide moles by 22.4 L/mol
Multiply moles by molar mass (g/mol)
distractorRationale: Inverts the operation; dividing gives mol²/g, which does not cancel to grams.
Uses Avogadro's number, which converts moles to particles, not to grams.
Uses the STP molar-volume constant, which converts moles to liters, not to grams.

items.stem: A student's units cancel to "mol²/g" instead of "mol." What should they do?
choices: Keep going; the arithmetic will still be correct
Redo the setup — the conversion factor was used upside down
Just relabel the final answer as "mol"
Ignore it — units only matter for gas problems
distractorRationale: Wrong units mean the setup, not just the label, is wrong — the arithmetic inherits the error.
Relabeling does not fix a wrong setup; the number itself is wrong.
The units check applies to every mole conversion, not only gas problems.

items.learningTarget: Sample size vs. amount of substance (S7.2)
items.stem: Sample X is 2.00 mol of neon gas. Sample Y is 2.00 mol of iron. Which statement is correct?
choices: Sample X contains more atoms because gases pack more particles per mole
Sample Y contains more atoms because iron is denser
Both samples contain the same number of atoms
It cannot be determined without knowing the temperature
distractorRationale: Confuses particle count with physical state; the mole fixes particle count regardless of state.
Confuses density with particle count.
Temperature affects volume for a gas, not the fixed particle count set by the mole.

day2.directions: Show every step of your work in the space provided. Carry units through every line. Circle your final answer with the correct units and significant figures. Partial credit is available — no credit is given for an answer with no work shown.

problems.prompt: Find the molar mass of MgCl₂. Show the sum, not just the final answer.
How many moles are in 68.0 g of MgCl₂?
What is the mass of 3.20 mol of CO₂?

workSteps: mass = 3.20 mol × 44.01 g/mol = 140.8 g → 141 g (3 sig figs)

problems.prompt: How many molecules are in 9.00 g of H₂O? This is two conversions — do them in order and do not skip the middle.
A sample of nitrogen gas (N₂) occupies 5.60 L at STP.
parts: a.  How many moles of N₂ are present?
b.  What is the mass of the sample?
c.  How many molecules of N₂ are present?
d.  A classmate claims that doubling the volume to 11.2 L would double the number of molecules. Using your work above, say whether they are correct and why.

answer.value: a. 0.250 mol   b. 7.01 g   c. 1.51 × 10²³ molecules   d. Correct — at STP, moles are directly proportional to volume (n = V ÷ 22.4), so doubling the volume doubles the moles and therefore doubles the number of molecules.
workSteps: b. molar mass N₂ = 2(14.01) = 28.02 g/mol; mass = 0.250 mol × 28.02 g/mol = 7.01 g
d. Direct proportionality: V → n → N all scale together at STP.

problems.prompt: Find the molar mass of Al₂O₃. Show the sum, not just the final answer.
How many moles are in 51.0 g of Al₂O₃?
What is the mass of 1.75 mol of NH₃?

workSteps: mass = 1.75 mol × 17.03 g/mol = 29.80 g → 29.8 g (3 sig figs)

problems.prompt: How many molecules are in 15.0 g of NaCl? This is two conversions — do them in order and do not skip the middle.
A sample of oxygen gas (O₂) occupies 8.96 L at STP.
parts: a.  How many moles of O₂ are present?
b.  What is the mass of the sample?
c.  How many molecules of O₂ are present?
d.  A classmate claims that cutting the volume in half to 4.48 L would cut the number of molecules in half. Using your work above, say whether they are correct and why.

answer.value: a. 0.400 mol   b. 12.8 g   c. 2.41 × 10²³ molecules   d. Correct — at STP, moles are directly proportional to volume (n = V ÷ 22.4), so halving the volume halves the moles and therefore halves the number of molecules.
workSteps: b. molar mass O₂ = 2(16.00) = 32.00 g/mol; mass = 0.400 mol × 32.00 g/mol = 12.8 g
d. Direct proportionality: V → n → N all scale together at STP.
